case_prompt: A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of an intermittent throbbing headache in the left temporal region that had worsened at night. She also noted bilateral temporal visual field defects. Her medical history was significant only for hypertension of more than 20 years; there was no personal or family history of autoimmune disease. On examination, her temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 140/108 mmHg, and neurologic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a serum potassium of 3.2 mmol/L, microscopic proteinuria, and a urinary specific gravity of 1.025. She was negative for antinuclear antibodies, immunoglobulin G (IgG), IgM, IgA, and IgG4, and had no antithyroid antibodies. Other biochemical and coagulation tests were within normal limits. Endocrine evaluation revealed deficiencies of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, thyroid axis, and gonadal axis. Chest CT was normal, and ECG showed flattened T waves. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland demonstrated symmetrical enlargement with suprasellar “dumbbell” extension, significant homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium, low signal in the anterior pituitary on T1, high signal on T2, a preserved bright spot in the posterior lobe, thickening of an undeviated pituitary stalk, bilateral cavernous sinus encirclement of the internal carotid arteries, and a parasellar dural tail sign.

sentences.text: A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of an intermittent throbbing headache in the left temporal region that had worsened at night.
She also noted bilateral temporal visual field defects.
Her medical history was significant only for hypertension of more than 20 years; there was no personal or family history of autoimmune disease.
On examination, her temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 140/108 mmHg, and neurologic examination was unremarkable.
Laboratory studies showed a serum potassium of 3.2 mmol/L, microscopic proteinuria, and a urinary specific gravity of 1.025.
She was negative for antinuclear antibodies, immunoglobulin G (IgG), IgM, IgA, and IgG4, and had no antithyroid antibodies.
Other biochemical and coagulation tests were within normal limits.
Endocrine evaluation revealed deficiencies of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, thyroid axis, and gonadal axis.
Chest CT was normal, and ECG showed flattened T waves.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland demonstrated symmetrical enlargement with suprasellar “dumbbell” extension, significant homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium, low signal in the anterior pituitary on T1, high signal on T2, a preserved bright spot in the posterior lobe, thickening of an undeviated pituitary stalk, bilateral cavernous sinus encirclement of the internal carotid arteries, and a parasellar dural tail sign.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Granulomatous hypophysitis considered because it can infiltrate the sella but excluded due to rarity and autopsy identification — “Although granulomatous hypophysitis could also present with similar sellar infiltration; however, granulomatous hypophysitis is very rare and often found by autopsy.” 2. Necrotizing hypophysitis considered but excluded by the presence of homogeneous contrast enhancement and absence of ischemic changes — “Necrotizing hypophysitis present with a lack of contrast enhancement and sudden-onset hypopituitarism… Our patient presented with marked homogeneous anterior pituitary enhancement without ischemic manifestations.” 3. Xanthomatous hypophysitis considered but excluded by the lack of cystic ring enhancement and known steroid responsiveness — “Xanthomatous hypophysitis commonly exhibits cystic enlargement and peripheral ring enhancement after contrast and is rarely known to improve in response to glucocorticoid therapies.”

selection.screen_reason: Headache and bitemporal field loss with hypopituitarism and a symmetrically enlarged, homogeneously enhancing pituitary with a thick stalk suggest lymphocytic hypophysitis.
selection.second_look_note: Headache and bitemporal field loss with anterior hypopituitarism and a symmetrically enlarged, homogeneously enhancing pituitary with a thick stalk point to lymphocytic hypophysitis.
